item.title: Coffee, Cigs, and Donuts
item.description:
Diet

Coffee, Cigs, and Donuts

What your brain craves.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Donuts provide the ingredients for making acetylcholine that is vital for learning and paying attention.
  • Caffeine is neuroprotective and prevents the inhibitory transmitter adenosine from turning off brain function.
  • Nicotine is neuroprotective and greatly reduces the risk of developing Parkinson’ disease.
  • Caffeine, sugar, and nicotine have all been shown to enhance cognitive function.

This is the main point of this post: Sometimes what your brain craves is not good for your body. We all know that this is true. We’re drawn to any food that has ample quantities of fat, salt, and sugar. Visit any coffee shop in the nation, and you’re likely to see people enjoying a cigarette with their coffee and glazed donut. Why do humans choose to consume chemicals that are so unhealthy? Smoking kills slowly and nicotine is incredibly toxic, caffeine is harmful to the heart muscles and, at high doses, can induce dangerous arrythmias, while the regular consumption of sugar-ladened donuts leads to diabetes and obesity-related disorders.

The reason is simple: Our brains reward us for consuming these foods/chemicals. [For a thorough discussion of this topic, go here: Your Brain on Food: How Chemicals Control Your Thoughts and Feelings.] It’s well known that nicotine, caffeine, and sugar produce euphoria which encourages their continued long-term use. However, science has clearly demonstrated their toxicity for our physical health; Is there any evidence that caffeine, nicotine, and sugar are beneficial to the brain? Yes. Let’s look at the evidence.

Donuts

It’s early morning and you’re having difficulty paying attention to the traffic, to the boss, to whatever you’re trying to accomplish. Why? Your brain is not cooperating because you just woke up that it’s low on one critical ingredient—sugar. You have been fasting since last night's dinner, and your blood levels of sugar have fallen. Sugar is indispensable. Your brain can’t function without it and will do whatever is necessary to convince you to eat sugar as soon as possible. Why?

Essentially, the presence of sugar in your brain is considered normal, and its absence leads to the craving—and to the initiation of foraging behaviors, such as seeking out a vending machine for cupcakes or a candy bar. There is a reason donut shops and sugar-laden cereals are so popular: You can lay the blame on neurons within the feeding center of your hypothalamus. If your brain did not want those donuts so badly, the shops would not be so densely distributed along your route to work.

Once inside the brain, sugar is also used to produce a very important neurotransmitter chemical called acetylcholine. Acetylcholine allows you to learn and remember, to regulate your attention and mood, and to control how well you can move. Your brain makes acetylcholine from choline. We frequently obtain choline in our diet by eating lecithin, which is present in donuts. Thus, a donut first thing in the morning is going to provide your brain with the sugar and choline it needs to pay attention and learn new things. Your big active brain utilizes the equivalent of 10 donuts worth of sugar every day.

Coffee

While you were dreaming during the few hours prior to waking up, your brain was burning through lots of energy molecules called ATP. All of the cells of your body require ATP to function. When ATP is consumed, the molecule “A” in the ATP falls away and begins to collect as debris. The “A” stands for adenosine. Unfortunately, as the levels of adenosine increases it begins to powerfully turn off your acetylcholine neurons. This is unfortunate because your brain cannot pay attention or learn new things if your acetylcholine neurons are turned off!

article continues after advertisement

What's the cure? Coffee. The caffeine in your coffee is able to prevent the actions of adenosine and release your acetylcholine neurons from their chemical shackles; your attentiveness improves and you are ready for anything—at least until the caffeine effect wears off. However, typical of just about everything we consume, a little caffeine is good but too much can kill you. Approximately five grams of caffeine—about 25 cups of coffee drank quickly—is a lethal dose for a typical adult. Consuming over 400 mg of caffeine (three espressos) daily increases susceptibility to cardiovascular disease. Chronic caffeine consumption may disturb the autonomic nervous system, leading to elevated blood pressure and heart rates that may predispose some vulnerable individuals to atrial fibrillation.

Human epidemiological studies consistently show that the risk of many age-related neurodegenerative diseases is reduced by chronic, moderate caffeine consumption. Forty years of clinical investigations have confirmed that the incidence of Parkinson’s disease is dose-dependently decreased (up to 85 percent!) as coffee consumption is increased to five cups per day (Tan et al., 2007).

Large epidemiological studies involving over hundreds of thousands of people consistently reported that coffee dose-dependently decreased the risk of brain tumors. The risk of brain gliomas, the most common type of brain tumor, decreased significantly when subjects drank more than three cups of coffee per day (Di Maso, et al., 2021). Coffee consumption was associated with a lower prevalence of small brain infarcts related to ischemic strokes. In addition to improving cognitive function, daily coffee consumption enhances the brain’s endogenous antioxidant systems.

Cigarettes

Humans have a complicated relationship with tobacco. Tobacco was once used to treat persistent headaches, colds, and abscesses or sores on the head. Tobacco enemas were used to treat flatulence, and even more surprising, the smoke was once inhaled deeply to lessen bad coughs. A cigarette made from tobacco will contain about 1 to 2 milligrams of nicotine. Because nicotine is quite volatile and heat labile, only about 20% of it is inhaled into the body. However, because of its exceptional lipid solubility, at least 90% of the inhaled nicotine is absorbed into the body. Sixty milligrams is considered a lethal dose for a human; death takes only a few minutes to occur and results from a loss of control of the nicotinic receptors on the diaphragm muscles.

article continues after advertisement

Nicotine is neuroprotective. Epidemiological studies consistently show an inverse association between smoking and the risk of developing Parkinson’s disease (Yang et al., 2025). Long-term, heavy smokers (who don’t die from lung cancer) have a significantly lower incidence of Parkinson’s disease as compared to non-smokers. This protective effect appears dose-dependent and diminishes after cessation, suggesting that ongoing nicotine exposure may be necessary to maintain the effect. Nicotine is likely the active component responsible for this reduced risk.

So, the next time you see someone enjoying a cigarette with their coffee and donut, congratulate them on working hard to keep their brain healthy.

item.title: What About Your Friends? What Nolan Wells Teaches Parents
item.description:
Friends

What About Your Friends? What Nolan Wells Teaches Parents

One teen's death is forcing a national conversation about friendship and race.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Being the "only one" in a friend group is a specific, nameable risk, not just an awkward social situation.
  • Black parents can teach kids language for naming tokenism and choosing safe, well-known spaces for sleepovers.
  • White parents can raise allies by teaching kids the words to use when a friend of color is excluded or blamed.
  • Racial socialization and reciprocal friendships are linked to lower anxiety and better identity development.

Y'all, I have to be honest with you. I have looked at all the pictures, watched all the videos, and re-read every headline and story about Nolan Wells, and every time, my stomach drops the same way it did the first time.

An 18-year-old goes out on a boat with a group he calls friends. Somewhere in those final hours, the stories stop matching up. One group says he chose to stay behind. Another says something else. And now a grand jury, a family attorney, concerned celebrities, forensic experts, and honestly, all of Beyonce’s internet are trying to piece together what actually happened to that baby.

I'm not writing this post to solve the case. I don't have that information and I’m not sure who does. But as a clinical psychologist who has spent almost fifteen years studying racial trauma and healing, and as a mom who has to send my own son, Roman, into a world full of friend groups I don't get to supervise, I keep coming back to one question that has nothing to do with what happened on that island and everything to do with the conversations we’re having about friendships, race, survival, and joy as our birthright: Does your child actually know how to tell a real friend from a convenient one?

Because here's what I notice every time I see a story like this in the therapy space, at a school, or on the news or social media. Somebody's kid was left behind. Somebody's kid didn't speak up. Somebody’s kid was harmed. Somebody's kid told a different story once the group was no longer together. And every time, parents across the country ask the same devastating question: Would my child's "friends" have done the same thing?

We spend so much of August buying bookbags and labeling folders and rehearsing "have a good day at school" that we skip the conversation that actually protects our kids and teaches them, concretely, what a real friend does and doesn't do.

Reciprocity, Not Proximity

In my training as a therapist, and now as a researcher and professor teaching the next generation of clinicians, I remind practitioners constantly: proximity is not intimacy, and popularity is not protection. A kid can be "in the group chat" and still be the one nobody speaks up for. Developmental research backs this up and shows that reciprocal friendships, the kind where a child consistently gets chosen back, correlate with lower anxiety and stronger identity development through adolescence. One-sided friendships, where a child is more invested than the group is in them, don't offer that same protection, even when they look identical from the outside.

So, before your child walks into a new classroom or sits at a new lunch table this fall, sit with them and ask: "Who checks on you when things go wrong? Who speaks up for you in front of others? Who tells the truth about you when you're not in the room?" That's the friendship test: not "Who do you sit with," but "Who would still be honest about you if it cost them something."

article continues after advertisement

Tips for Black (or Other Marginalized) Parents: Naming the "Only One" Danger Out Loud

Growing up, my parents had a rule that used to embarrass me: I was only allowed to sleep over at my family's houses: real family, play cousins, godparents, and other extended family who had known me since I was in diapers. At the time, I thought it was overprotective. Now that I'm the one raising a son, I understand exactly what they were doing. They weren't just being strict. They were making sure that if something ever went wrong in the middle of the night, the adults in that house already loved me and already had reason to tell the truth about what happened to me.

Source: Isha W. Metzger

That's the lesson I want to give Roman, and it's the lesson I want to hand you, plainly:

  • Give racism a name before school does. Kids will encounter racist jokes, racist assumptions, or racist treatment whether or not you've prepared them. Naming it clearly at home means they recognize it the first time it happens instead of the fifth.
  • Teach them to notice who speaks up and who stays quiet. In a mixed group, ask your child: when something goes wrong, who tells the adults what really happened to you, and who lets someone else's version become the story?
  • Set concrete rules for overnight and unsupervised situations, the way my parents did with me, and say the "why" out loud instead of just enforcing the rule silently. "You can sleep over at a house of people we know well, because I want grown-ups in that house who already love you" is a sentence a child can carry with them.
  • Give them exit language for tokenized spaces: "I felt like I was there to be the target of jokes, not because they had my back" is a feeling an eight- or nine-year-old can learn to name and bring home to you.
  • Celebrate the differences, don't just survive them. Being the only one in a room doesn't have to mean shrinking. Talk with your child about what it means to bring your full self (like, your language, your hair, your music, your family's traditions) into a friend group instead of changing yourself to fit in.

This isn't about raising suspicious kids or isolated kids. It's about raising kids who know the difference between being included and being valued, and kids who know that "I'm the only one here who looks like me" is information worth paying attention to, not something to ignore.

Tips for White (or, Majority) Parents: Raising Kids Who Know How to Be an Ally

article continues after advertisement

This part matters just as much, and it's the part that gets skipped most often. White children need direct, explicit coaching in how to actually be an ally to their Black friends. They don’t need colorblind or vague "be kind to everyone" messaging, but specific, rehearsed language for the exact moment a Black (or other marginalized) friend is being excluded, blamed, tokenized, or left to explain themselves alone.

Source: Isha W. Metzger
  • Teach the word and the sentence, not just the sentiment. "That’s racist, “That's not fair, let's go find them" or "She wasn't even there, why are we blaming her" are sentences a six- or seven-year-old can practice and use. Kids can spot "that's not fair" faster than they can spot racism, so we should teach both the sentiment and the word. Teach kids that racism is not just slurs and name-calling, but who gets blamed, who gets included, who gets excluded, who gets left to explain themselves.
  • Explain what tokenizing looks like from the outside, so your child can recognize when a friend is being included as "the only one" rather than as a full member of the group, and can actively work to change that instead of benefiting from it.
  • Normalize speaking up even when it costs social capital. An ally isn't the kid who agrees quietly afterward. It's the kid who says something while the group is still watching.
  • Celebrate differences with your kids at home, out loud, so noticing and naming a friend's culture, hair, food, or traditions feels natural and respectful rather than awkward or invisible.

Silence in difficult moments isn't neutral. It's a choice. And staying vague about racism so it "stays age-appropriate" is its own kind of silence that causes harm. Racial socialization research is clear that these conversations, in both Black and white households, are protective. They are not the things that create division. Silence is.

Before the Bookbags

This school year, before you get to the "don't talk to strangers" talk, have the "who talks about you when you're not there" talk. Role-play it. Ask your kid to name one friend who has already shown, in a real moment, that they'd tell the truth for them. If they can't name one yet, that's not a failure, it's information, and it can be taught while teaching our kids how to recognize (and be) good friends.

Nolan Wells' family is still waiting for answers none of us can give them. What we can give our own kids is a clearer understanding of racism and a clearer definition of loyalty before they need it.
